title: Max Sum of Rectangle No Larger Than K
description: Brute force to optimized: enumerating every rectangle via 2D prefix sums versus fixing column pairs, collapsing to 1D, and using sorted prefix sums to respect the cap on k.

sections.title: Max Sum of Rectangle No Larger Than K

content.title: Max Sum of Rectangle No Larger Than K

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given a rows by cols integer matrix and an integer k, find the maximum possible sum of any rectangular submatrix, subject to that sum being no larger than k. It is guaranteed that at least one rectangle has a sum no larger than k.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","matrix (rows x cols integers), k"],["Output","The maximum rectangle sum that does not exceed k"],["Goal","Search efficiently, without recomputing every rectangle sum from raw cells"],["Constraints","rows, cols <= 100; matrix[i][j], k fit in a signed 32-bit range"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A rectangle is defined by 4 corners in a 2D grid","2D prefix sums, so any rectangle's sum is a handful of lookups instead of re-summing every cell"],["The rectangle can span any set of rows, once the column range is fixed","Collapsing a column range down to one sum per row, turning the 2D search into a 1D one"],["The best 1D subarray sum must stay under a cap, not simply be the maximum","A sorted running set of prefix sums, so the tightest prefix under the cap can be found quickly"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a matrix and an integer k, find a rectangular block of cells, any width and any height, whose sum is as large as possible while staying at or below k.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Best Budget-Constrained Purchase
blocks.text: Picture a grid of item values, some negative (discounts), some positive (costs), and needing to select a rectangular block of them that gets as close to a budget k as possible without going over.

blocks.caption: A 2D prefix sum grid turns any rectangle sum into 4 corner lookups

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
The best rectangle is the single cell [1] (top-left) plus [0] beneath it, or the single cell [1] alone, either way the best achievable sum without exceeding k is 2.
Example: matrix = [[2,2,-1]], k = 3
The two-cell rectangle [2,2] sums to 4, which exceeds k, so the best valid rectangle is a single cell, giving 3.
Edge case: every value is already at most k
When the sum of the entire matrix does not exceed k, the entire matrix itself is the best rectangle.
5. How Should We Think?
Before checking every possible rectangle directly, notice that once a specific left and right column boundary is fixed, the problem collapses from 2D down to a much simpler 1D one.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For a fixed pair of columns, summing across just those columns for every row produces one number per row, exactly the shape of the "maximum subarray sum no more than k" problem in 1D.

Observation 2: A 1D prefix sum makes any row-range sum, within that fixed column pair, a single subtraction between two prefix values.

Observation 3: To keep a subarray sum at or below k while maximizing it, for the current prefix, the best earlier prefix to subtract is the smallest one that is still at least (current prefix minus k).

Observation 4: Keeping every earlier prefix sum in sorted order lets that smallest-qualifying-value be found quickly instead of scanning all of them again for every row.
Fixing every possible pair of column boundaries, and solving the resulting 1D "best sum under a cap" problem with a sorted set of prefixes, avoids ever re-summing a rectangle's raw cells.
6. Brute Force Solution
Build a 2D prefix sum so any rectangle's sum is a fixed number of lookups, then check every possible rectangle directly against k.
Step by step algorithm

items: Build a 2D prefix sum grid, where prefix[i][j] holds the sum of the rectangle from the top-left corner to (i minus 1, j minus 1).
For every pair of a top-left corner and a bottom-right corner, compute that rectangle's sum using 4 lookups into the prefix grid.
If the sum is at most k, compare it against the best sum found so far.
Return the best qualifying sum after checking every rectangle.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: every rectangle, checked directly against k

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The 2D prefix grid is padded with an extra row and column of zeros, so every rectangle, including ones touching row or column 0, uses the same 4-lookup formula with no special casing.
All four corner boundaries are looped independently, so every one of the roughly (rows times cols) squared rectangles gets checked exactly once.
The sum-at-most-k condition is applied directly to each rectangle as it is computed.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Dry run intuition

blocks.content: {"headers":["Rectangle count","Why it grows this fast"],"rows":[["Roughly (rows choose 2) times (cols choose 2)","Every pair of row boundaries combines with every pair of column boundaries, a 4-way nested choice"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows squared times cols squared), every rectangle is enumerated explicitly.
Space: O(rows times cols) for the 2D prefix grid.

Limitation: once a pair of column boundaries is fixed, the remaining work is really a 1D problem, best sum within a cap, over one number per row, but the brute force still re-explores every row boundary pair from scratch for every column pair.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why re-checking every row pair per column pair is wasteful: for a fixed column range, the row-boundary search is just "best subarray sum at most k" on a 1D array, and that has its own efficient solution using prefix sums and a sorted set.

What replaces the inner double loop over rows: compress each row down to its sum across the fixed column range, producing a single 1D array, one number per row.

How to find the best sum at most k on that 1D array: keep every prefix sum seen so far in sorted order; for the current prefix, the best earlier prefix to subtract is the smallest one at least (current prefix minus k), found by binary search.

The core idea: fix every pair of column boundaries, collapse rows into one sum per row for that range, then solve a 1D capped-maximum-subarray problem using sorted prefix sums.

For each pair of left and right column boundaries, build a 1D array of row sums restricted to that column range. Walk that array while maintaining a sorted set of prefix sums seen so far; at each row, binary search for the smallest earlier prefix at least (current prefix minus k), and use it to get the best qualifying subarray ending at that row.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for one column range

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row prefix so far","Sorted earlier prefixes","Best sum <= k using this prefix"],"rows":[["First row prefix","just 0","prefix minus 0, if that is at most k"],["Second row prefix","0 and the first prefix","prefix minus the smallest earlier prefix that keeps the result at most k"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: fix columns, collapse to 1D, use sorted prefixes to respect the cap

blocks.text: Why This Works

For a fixed column range, prefix minus some earlier prefix gives exactly the sum of the rows strictly between them; requiring that difference to be at most k, and maximizing it, is the same as finding the smallest earlier prefix that is still at least (current prefix minus k). Keeping every earlier prefix in sorted order lets that lookup happen in logarithmic time instead of scanning every earlier row again.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(cols squared times rows times log(rows)), one row-collapsing pass plus a sorted-set lookup per row, for every pair of column boundaries.
Space: O(rows) for the row sums and the sorted set of prefixes.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (every rectangle via 2D prefix sums)","O(rows squared times cols squared)","O(rows times cols)","Correct, but explores far more rectangles than necessary."],["Optimized (fix columns, sorted 1D prefixes)","O(cols squared times rows times log(rows))","O(rows)","The expected answer; a genuine complexity class improvement whenever cols is smaller than rows."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

This problem is a direct combination of two ideas already used elsewhere on this sheet: 2D-to-1D reduction by fixing one dimension's boundaries, and a sorted-prefix-sum technique for capped subarray sums. Recognizing that a fixed column range turns the search into a familiar 1D problem is the key insight.
Common Mistakes

items: Iterating over every rectangle directly instead of collapsing a fixed column range into a 1D row-sum array first.
Searching for the largest earlier prefix instead of the smallest one that is still at least (current prefix minus k).
Forgetting to seed the sorted set of prefixes with 0, which represents "no rows subtracted yet."

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["The entire matrix sums to at most k","The whole matrix is the best rectangle."],["Every value is negative and k is negative","The best rectangle is still whichever single cell (or block) comes closest to k without exceeding it."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explicitly stating the reduction, fix a column range, collapse to 1D, solve the capped-maximum-subarray problem with sorted prefixes, demonstrates the full chain of reasoning rather than jumping straight to a memorized solution.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid enumerating every rectangle", think: fix a column range, and reduce the row search to a 1D problem.
If the interviewer says "how do you keep the sum under a cap while maximizing it", think: a sorted set of prefix sums, searching for the smallest one still large enough to keep the result under the cap.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does fixing columns instead of rows matter for the final time complexity, and when would you swap them?
How would you adapt this solution if the matrix could be updated between queries?
Can you find the actual rectangle's coordinates, not just its sum, with this same approach?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Prefix Sum problems that search for a capped or targeted subarray sum using a sorted or hashed set of earlier prefixes.
Matrix problems that reduce a 2D search to 1D by fixing one pair of boundaries and collapsing the other dimension.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(rows squared times cols squared) time and O(rows times cols) space. The optimized approach runs in O(cols squared times rows times log(rows)) time and O(rows) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a 2D-to-1D reduction, fixing one pair of boundaries and collapsing the other dimension, combined with a sorted-prefix-sum search for a capped maximum.
Core Idea: fix every pair of column boundaries, collapse each row into a single sum for that range, then use sorted prefix sums to find the best row-range sum that stays at most k.
Time: O(rows squared times cols squared) for the brute force, O(cols squared times rows times log(rows)) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(rows times cols) for the brute force's 2D prefix grid, O(rows) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: fixing one pair of boundaries turns a 2D rectangle search into a familiar 1D capped-subarray-sum problem.
Interview Difficulty: the 2D prefix sum brute force is straightforward; the sorted-prefix reduction to 1D is the harder, higher-value insight.
One line memory trick: fix the columns, collapse to one row-sum array, then hunt the tightest prefix under the cap.
